1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4.strategy: Recaptures at once, and the queen takes the central square, so White holds the whole centre for now. The cost is an early queen that Black can attack with a developing move: White spends tempi for space and a simple, safe position.
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4.name: Centre Game

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3.strategy: Brings a piece to bear on d4 and prepares to recapture with a knight, so the queen stays at home. The pawn is not retaken at once, so Black can hold it for a while; the game is open, with ordinary development and no early queen exposure.
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3.name: Centre Game: Kieseritzky Variation
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3.background: Lionel Kieseritzky played this line in a blind simultaneous display in 1851, and published the game, with his own notes, in La Régence, the chess journal he edited.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Bc4.strategy: Develops the bishop straight at f7 and delays the recapture, planning to retake on d4 with a piece rather than the queen. White plays for quick development against the pawn; Black must watch f7, guarded only by the king, in an open, fast game.
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Bc4.name: Centre Game: von der Lasa Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Bc4.background: Older chess works refer to 3.Bc4 as the Centre Gambit.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3.strategy: Offers a pawn, or even two, for quick development and open lines against Black's king. Black may take, strike back in the centre or decline, and White's pieces come out easily in each case; but with care Black keeps the material, so it is a surprise weapon rather than a main line.
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3.name: Danish Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3.background: Hans Lindehn played it regularly from 1857 at the latest, but the Danish player Martin Severin From, who played it at the Paris tournament of 1867, is usually given credit, and the gambit is named for him. It was popular with masters of the attack such as Alekhine, Marshall, Blackburne and Mieses, but lost favour in the 1920s as Black's defences improved, and it is rarely played at top level today.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.f4.strategy: A pawn sacrifice that loosens White's own king before a piece has moved, since the f-pawn leaves the diagonal leading to e1. White hopes for a broad centre and quick development, but Black keeps the extra pawn and develops freely.
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.f4.name: Centre Game: Halasz-McDonnell Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.f4.background: The move 3.f4 dates back to at least 1840, and it was championed more recently by the Hungarian correspondence player György Halasz. It has been described as dubious, but it has not been definitively refuted.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Bd3.strategy: Develops the bishop but puts it on the d-file, where it blocks the queen's way to d4 and leaves the pawn unattacked. White is simply a pawn down with no quick way to win it back or open lines, while Black develops at leisure.
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Bd3.name: Centre Game: Ross Gambit

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 d5.strategy: The best way to meet the gambit: a central counterblow that gives the extra pawn straight back, so White's lead in development has no material to attack with. The game is open and level, though Black's queen comes out early and has to be handled with care.
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 d5.name: Danish Gambit Declined: Sörensen Defence

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 dxc3.name: Danish Gambit Accepted
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 dxc3.strategy: Takes the pawn and goes a pawn up, at the price of letting White develop with tempo against the king. With care it is safe, and analysis even gives Black a slight edge, but the accepted gambit is dangerous in practice because White's pieces come out with threats.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 Ne7.strategy: Declines by developing the knight, which covers d5, f5 and g6 but does nothing about the pawn on c3. White simply retakes in the centre with a pawn and gets a broad pawn centre and space; Black is solid but passive.
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 Ne7.name: Danish Gambit Accepted: Svenonius Defence

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.f4 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop and guards the d4 pawn, so Black simply keeps the extra pawn while White's king position stays loosened. Black has no need to hurry or to take risks.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop to its most active square and defends d4, but the pawn cannot be held: White simply retakes with the knight, and the game becomes an open one with level material and natural development for both sides.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3 c5.name: Centre Game: Kieseritzky Variation
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3 c5.strategy: Holds the d4 pawn with a pawn, but at a cost: no pawn can ever guard d5 again and White's pieces come out first. Black keeps the extra pawn, and White's play is on the weakened squares in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6.name: Centre Game: Normal Variation
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6.strategy: Attacks the queen and develops in the same move, so White has to move the queen a second time. Black gains a tempo and takes the initiative in development, while White keeps the centre and a space advantage.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Bc4.strategy: Offers a second pawn instead of recapturing quietly with the knight: the bishop aims at f7 and White puts development before material. If Black takes, White's bishops open fire down the board, and the idea is a decisive lead in development.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Bc4 cxb2.strategy: Takes the second pawn: Black is two pawns up, and White has to recapture with the bishop, which lands on the long diagonal. The extra material is real, but Black must finish development and hand some of it back at the right moment.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Bc4 cxb2 5.strategy: Recaptures and puts the bishop on the long diagonal against g7, next to the bishop on c4 aimed at f7. White is two pawns down for a big lead in development, so the attack has to bring concrete gains before Black consolidates.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Bc4 cxb2 5.name: Danish Gambit Accepted: Schlechter Defence
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Bc4 cxb2 5.background: Carl Schlechter recommended it as one of the most reliable defences for Black. After it was introduced, the Danish Gambit's popularity fell sharply, because the positions it leads to are not what White wants from a gambit.
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Bc4 cxb2 5.strategy: Gives one pawn back to free the c8-bishop and the queen and to break White's grip on the centre; the pawn also attacks the bishop on c4. Black completes development and heads for a level, often queenless game, with the queenside majority a long-term asset.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Bc4 cxb2 5.name: Danish Gambit Accepted: Classical Defence
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Bc4 cxb2 5.strategy: Develops with an attack on e4 and invites 6.e5, which seems to trap the knight but runs into ...d5, hitting the bishop in return. Black prefers piece play and quick development to returning a pawn, at the price of a tactical game.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Bc4 cxb2 5.name: Danish Gambit Accepted: Copenhagen Defence
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Bc4 cxb2 5.strategy: Develops with check and so gains a tempo, forcing White to block or move the king before attacking on. The bishop on b4 can later be harassed by the queen from b3, where it also adds to the pressure on f7.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Bc4 cxb2 5.name: Danish Gambit Accepted: Chigorin Defence
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Bc4 cxb2 5.strategy: Hits the e4 pawn but sits in front of the king's bishop, so the kingside stays undeveloped while both white bishops already point at f7 and g7. It adds nothing to Black's development, which is the one thing Black cannot spare against this attack.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.f4 Bc5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops with an attack on d4 and covers h4, so Black's queen can no longer use the weakened diagonal. White now puts real pressure on the extra pawn, and Black must defend it with developing moves.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.f4 Bc5 4.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Defends d4 a second time with a developing move and keeps the extra pawn. Black stays ahead in development, the king can castle soon, and White's gambit has bought nothing concrete yet.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.f4 Bc5 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.c.name: Centre Game: Halasz-McDonnell Gambit, Crocodile Variation
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.f4 Bc5 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.c.strategy: Attacks d4 a third time, three attackers against two defenders, so Black must decide whether to hold, take or push. White offers a second pawn to rebuild a pawn centre and open lines, a risky way to keep the gambit going.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3 Bc5 4.c3.name: Centre Game: Lanc-Arnold Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3 Bc5 4.c3.strategy: A pawn offer instead of simply retaking: White opens lines for quick development and wants a pawn centre later, and Black is a pawn up without an obvious debt. The compensation is development and open lines rather than anything concrete.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3 Bc5 4.c3 dxc3.strategy: Takes the pawn and is now two pawns up. White's compensation is development, so Black has to finish developing quickly and give material back before the white pieces coordinate.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3 Bc5 4.c3 dxc3 5..name: Centre Game: Lanc-Arnold Gambit, Schippler Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3 Bc5 4.c3 dxc3 5..strategy: Gives the b-pawn too, as the bishop takes its best diagonal, and White plays for development and open lines against a king that has not castled. The sacrifice is purely dynamic: Black has to develop safely and return material at the right moment.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3 c5 4.Bc4.name: Centre Game: Kieseritzky Variation
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3 c5 4.Bc4.strategy: Develops the bishop at f7, defended only by the king, while the knight keeps the d4 pawn under attack. Black's c-pawn holds d4 but leaves d5 unguarded for White's bishop and pieces, so Black has to meet the pressure accurately.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qe3.name: Centre Game: Paulsen Attack Variation
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qe3.background: By far the most popular retreat for White's queen.
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qe3.strategy: The queen guards e4, lines up with Black's king on the e-file and makes ...d5 awkward. White accepts a lag in development for a firm centre, with the queen ready to swing to g3 against g7.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qc4.name: Centre Game: Hall Variation
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qc4.strategy: Keeps the queen on the diagonal towards f7 and still guards e4 along the fourth rank. A less explored alternative, but ...d5 attacks the queen at once, so White needs an answer ready; Black has chances to gain time in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qe3 Nf6.name: Centre Game: Berger Variation
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qe3 Nf6.strategy: The usual reply: Black develops, hits the e4 pawn and prepares to castle. Black is ahead in development and keeps ...d5 in reserve, so White has to defend e4 and catch up with pieces.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qe3 Bb4+.strategy: Develops with check along the diagonal to the king, forcing White to block or move the king before developing. Black keeps a flexible position and gives the bishop a job at once.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qe3 f5.name: Centre Game: l'Hermet Variation
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qe3 f5.strategy: Attacks e4 but weakens Black's own king: 5.exf5+ opens the e-file with check, and White's queen is already lined up on it. Black is left with a loosened kingside and a harassed king for no clear gain.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qe3 Bb4+.strategy: Meets the check with a pawn that also attacks the bishop; the queen guards it, so Black's bishop has to move. The price is that the knight loses its natural square on c3, and the pawn move does not help development.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qe3 Bb4+.name: Centre Game: Charousek Variation
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qe3 Bb4+.strategy: Retreats the bishop to a safe square, where it still helps castling, and leaves White with a pawn on c3 that has taken the knight's natural square. Black gets a compact position and prepares a central strike.

1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qe3 Nf6 5.strategy: The traditional move: it defends e4 with a developing move, which frees the queen from guard duty and keeps the pieces active. White aims for queenside castling and a kingside attack with the queen swinging to g3.
Pins the knight to the king, so e4 is guarded only by the queen and White has to deal with the pin. Black develops with tempo and aims at the e4 pawn and the open e-file.
Breaks the pin with a developing move, so the knight again guards e4, and clears the back rank for castling long. White then plans to swing the queen to the kingside against g7.

Castles into safety before the middlegame sharpens, with the rook ready for the e-file, where it aims at e4 and the queen. White usually castles long, so the kings stand on opposite wings and each side attacks the other's king.
